translation:
Palasvada

Santdas, a disciple of Jivanji Maharaj, established a gadi (spiritual seat) in this village. Since there proved to be no heir to it, an heir from Gyaniji Maharaj's own family, from Mota Sanja, now occupies this gadi. Gyaniji Maharaj's gadi has thus been established there, and near the temple there are seven tulsi-kyaras (raised tulsi-plant beds); one of these is likely Santdasji's. Jagdishchandra Jugaldas Maharaj, the last to occupy this gadi, used to say that among these tulsi-kyaras there is also likely one belonging to Raghunathdasji, who was born within Gyaniji Maharaj's lineage. Thus this place holds the memory both of Gyaniji Maharaj and of Santdasji, the disciple of Jivanji Maharaj, and moreover has these tulsi-kyaras. This is how tulsi-kyaras are found within our own tradition — as at Patan, Mota Sanja, Palasvad, Puniyad, Sabalpur, Sardarpur, Bodeli, Hansapura, Amadara, Tandalja, and elsewhere. For this reason, this

Palasvad is, for us, a closely-connected and important holy place.

At Patra, in the satsang gathering held at the home of devotee Lakshmanbhai Raghunathbhai, a reckoning of Jivanji Maharaj's gadis is set down on page 64 [of that record].

On page 1577 of that same gathering's record _[unclear]_, is written the account concerning Jivan['s authority] (the passage here is too damaged to render with confidence). This is followed by the sakhi of Visram Bija, of the lineage of Rankavanka:

_[unclear — the couplet itself is too badly garbled in the source to transliterate or translate reliably.]_

The truth of this saying is borne out by this very gathering — that many people have had parcha (a manifest sign) of Jivandasji.

(1) Malva; (2) _[unclear]_, son of a devotee of Pransvadi-Dhaman; (3) _[unclear]_ — this is indeed the gadi at Surat itself; (4) Sardarpur — from among these _[the rest of this sentence is too garbled to render reliably]_.

Their names: first, the Vaishnav of Malva, Gopaldas Santdas, of Chanderiya village — the gadi in Malva continues through him. Further, Santdasji came to Gujarat to join Jivandasji. He took up residence in the village of Paransvada and carried forward the tradition (nad) there — that is the second gadi.

Then, when Vaishnavji [Jivandasji] came to reside at Mangleshwar, the spirit of Bhoja Gujar had entered the body of Rambai, wife of Keshavdas Zadeshariya; he delivered her from it. Through this, devotion arose in Keshavdas Soni, and he made people of the villages of Surat pargana into Vaishnavs, carrying the tradition forward as a gadi in Surat.

In the village of Puniyad, Vaishnavji used to bring about Hari-parcha (manifest signs of the Divine) at satsang gatherings; in that connection, Krishnadasji, a worshipper of Ganesh, came to him, and Vaishnavji, in his grace, gave him the mala (rosary) and tilak; his gadi continues in the village of Vijapur, in Sardarpur pargana.

When Vaishnavji departed for his heavenly abode (sadham), at the gathering held on that occasion the Vaishnavs assembled together. Among them was the Vaishnav Kanhandasji, humble and wholly devoted. Vaishnavji, upon seeing him, showed very great grace and placed his own neck-mala upon Kanhandasji, entrusting him with the dharma of the tradition; this was accepted by all the Vaishnavs present, who then paid homage to Kanhandasji. Then the Vaishnavs of that assembly, finding Samdasji to be exceedingly discerning, and recognising him as a revered, manifest form born of Vaishnavji's own body, made repeated entreaty to Vaishnavji, saying: "The service (tehel) of this seat has been entrusted to Kanhandasji, but should Samdasji remain in your household, then, by the will of the Vaishnavs present, the dharma of the household-tradition belongs to him." Hearing this, Vaishnavji, through Kanhandasji, graciously entrusted the service to Samdasji as well; and the gadi of Samdasji's family continues in the village of Puniyad.

Samdasji's son, Dwarkadasji, received the mala and tilak from Vaishnavji in his presence, along with the Naha Parekh. Later, when they met again at a satsang gathering, it was affirmed that this is the eternal (sanatan) dharma of the tradition. But because Dwarkadasji began to carry on the practice of dharma while harbouring a hidden self-interest, Parakhji's mind was wounded, and he asked for a word of the guru's grace; Dwarkadasji granted it. He then went and settled in the village of Darapara, and fulfilled the words of the true guru, Bhakti-Satguru Jivandasji; many devotees came there to meet him, and to them, with grace, he revealed the Vaishnav dharma — that is another gadi.

6. Darapara, 7. Hansapura — these [two gadis] continue to this day.

In their lineage is Ratanji Bhanaji; in that household was Samdas Ratanji, who became the leading figure (narsaiyo) of their dharma. Further, upon Samdasji's gadi there came to sit the head (swami) of the Bund lineage. He carried himself with an attitude of self-importance, on account of which the Vaishnavs suffered distress. Then, at the village of Sahapar, there was an old, established temple of the Vaishnavs; recognising this, it was made into a place of rest (visram). That gadi was carried on by entrusting its service to Mohandas Swami, son of Vitthaldas Swami — but it is not accompanied by parcha (manifest divine proof); it appears to carry on merely the customary rites pertaining to the body/lineage.

In this way, seven gadis have come to be known up to this day, and they have been described and set down here in writing. Further, should any Vaishnav come to learn more, let this seventh and final gadi be expanded upon accordingly.

In the family of Parakhji, holder of the sixth gadi, is Ratanji Bhanji. He had four sons: (1) Kanhandas, (2) Keshavdas, (3) Samdas, and (4) Dialdas — the last born of a different mother; his own sons numbered three: the eldest, Laldas Mohota; the second, Harjivandas; the third, Jagjivandas. On account of Jagjivandas, Laldas Mohota performed an act of renunciation (khovatpanu) — regarding which there is this sakhi:
